title: Poets and painters
hookLine: Sengai's circle-triangle-square, Ryokan's poems, thangka painters

lines: A CIRCLE, A TRIANGLE, A SQUARE.
cards: Three shapes in black ink: a circle, a triangle and a square, overlapping, drawn quickly with a wet brush. Beside them, a short line of writing that names the painter's temple and explains nothing.
The Zen monk Sengai painted it in Japan, and people still argue about what it means. Some see the whole universe in it. Some see the schools of Buddhism.
Some just see a monk having fun with a brush.

teach.h: SENGAI: A PUZZLE WITH NO ANSWER.
teach.b: Sengai was a Zen abbot who painted loose, funny, warm pictures: frogs sitting in meditation, monks laughing, plain shapes.
He left no explanation of his circle, triangle and square, and that silence may be the teaching: the picture doesn't hand you an answer, it hands you a question to sit with, the way a koan does.
Then Ryokan, the poet-monk this path met earlier, playing with children and pitying a thief.
He wrote short poems in plain words about his begging rounds, rain on his hut, an empty bowl, falling leaves. Nothing grand.
The practice is in the attention: he notices small things so fully that the poem feels like a sitting written down. Then go west, to the Himalayas, to the thangka painters of Tibet.
A thangka is a painting on cloth, usually of a buddha, a bodhisattva or a mandala, made to be used in practice: hung in a shrine, looked at in meditation. Here there's no loose brushwork.
The painter follows careful grids and set proportions, handed down from teacher to student, so every line is in its place.
Some painters recite and keep vows while they work, and the finished painting may be consecrated before it's hung.
Three very different ways to make art as practice: Sengai's playful ink, Ryokan's plain words, the thangka painter's exact lines.
One loose, one quiet, one precise.
What they share is attention, poured into the brush or the word until the work itself becomes a kind of sitting.

how: In Zen, monks and lay students practice brush painting and calligraphy, including the ink circle; in Tibetan Buddhism, thangka painters train with a master for years, follow set proportions, and paintings are consecrated before use in shrines and meditation.

games.q: you're Sengai. you've painted a circle, a triangle and a square. what do you write beside it?
o: only a line naming your temple
games.why: the only writing beside it names his temple. the picture hands you a question to sit with, like a koan.

practice: With any pen and scrap of paper, or a finger on your palm, draw a single circle slowly, paying attention to the whole movement: the start, the curve, where it closes or doesn't.
Don't fix it; look at it, and if there's time, add a triangle, then a square, each one its own small sitting. It doesn't have to be good, only done with attention.

wordCard.voice: Enso. The Zen ink circle Sengai drew, alongside Ryokan's plain poems and the thangka painter's exact lines: teachers whose art was practice.

orig.note: Japanese enso: the Zen ink circle, often drawn in a single stroke.

carryVoice: Your line: practice in art. Loose, quiet or precise, the attention is the same. Rest well.
